## What is R?

R is an open-source interpreted functional programming language (with OO elements) used for statistics and data analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Vectors & Arrays

There are 6 atomic data types in R:

| Type | Description | Example |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| **Double** | Double-precision floating-point numbers | `3.14`, `42.0` |
| **Integer** | Whole numbers (denoted explicitly with an `L` suffix) | `42L`, `-7L` |
| **Character** | Strings | `"hello"`, `'data'` |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Type | Description | Example |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Logical** | Boolean values | `TRUE`, `FALSE` (or `T`, `F`) |
| **Complex** | Numbers with real and imaginary parts | `2 + 3i` |
| **Raw** | Raw bytes / hexadecimal values | `as.raw(42)` |

> **Note:** "Numeric" is a superclass that combines both **Double** and **Integer**.

> **Note:** All scalars in R are simply 1-dimensional vectors.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Atomic Vectors

Can only contain elements of the same data type.

Created using the combine function `c()`.

``` r
x <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)
x
# [1] 10 20 30 40
```

The combine function automatically flattens nested vectors:

``` r
x <- c(c(1, 2), c(3, 4))
x
# [1] 1 2 3 4
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Coercion

Because atomic vectors can only contain elements of a single data type, R automatically converts (coerces) elements if you attempt to combine different types together.

### The coercion hierarchy

Logical -\> Integer -\> Double (Numeric) -\> Complex -\> Character

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Examples

Logical and Integer -\> Integer (`TRUE` becomes 1)

``` r
c(TRUE, 5L)
#> [1] 1 5
```

Integer and Numeric -\> Double (Numeric)

``` r
c(1L, 2.5)
#> [1] 1.0 2.5
```

Numeric and Character -\> Character

``` r
c(1, 2.5, "apple")
#> [1] "1"     "2.5"   "apple"
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Assignment operators

| Operator | Meaning                                         |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `<-`     | Assign right to left                            |
| `=`      | Assign right to left                            |
| `<<-`    | Global (parent environment) assignment operator |
| `->`     | Left-to-right version of `<-`                   |
| `->>`    | Left-to-right version of `<<-`                  |

### Example

``` r
mu <- 5
sigma = 2
10 -> n
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The difference between `<-` and `=` shows up inside function calls:

``` r
mean(x = c(1, 2, 3))   # x is an argument name; no variable x is created
x                      # Error: object 'x' not found 

mean(x <- c(1, 2, 3))  # assigns x in your workspace AND passes it on
x
# [1] 1 2 3
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Operators

Most operators in R work on vectors element-wise.

#### Arithmetic operators

| Operator | Meaning            | Example   | Result |
|----------|--------------------|-----------|--------|
| `+`      | Addition           | `5 + 2`   | 7      |
| `-`      | Subtraction        | `5 - 2`   | 3      |
| `*`      | Multiplication     | `5 * 2`   | 10     |
| `/`      | Division           | `5 / 2`   | 2.5    |
| `^`      | Exponent           | `5 ^ 2`   | 25     |
| `%%`     | Modulo (remainder) | `5 %% 2`  | 1      |
| `%/%`    | Integer division   | `5 %/% 2` | 2      |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

When vectors have different lengths, the shorter one is **recycled**:

``` r
c(1, 2, 3, 4) * c(10, 100)
#> [1]  10 200 30 400
```

R warns you if the longer length isn't a multiple of the shorter one:

``` r
c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20)
# [1] 11 22 13
# Warning message:
# In c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20) :
# longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object length
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Comparison

Comparison operators return logical vectors: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.

``` r
x <- c(5, 10, 15, NA)
x > 8
#> [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE NA
x == 10
#> [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE NA
```

Most comparison involving `NA` returns `NA`, because R can't know the answer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Logical

| Operator | Meaning      | Works on               |
|----------|--------------|------------------------|
| `!`      | NOT          | vectors                |
| `&`      | AND          | vectors (element-wise) |
| `|`      | OR           | vectors (element-wise) |
| `xor()`  | Exclusive OR | vectors                |
| `&&`     | AND          | single values only     |
| `||`   | OR           | single values only     |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Examples

``` r
age <- c(22, 35, 41, 58)
age > 30 & age < 50
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE
age < 25 | age > 55
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE
!(age > 30)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Comments:

Use `&&` and `||` in `if` conditions, where you need a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
Use `&` and `|` when filtering vectors.

Logical values are treated as 0 and 1 in arithmetic, which gives you counts and
proportions:

``` r
sum(age > 30)    # how many
#> [1] 3

mean(age > 30)   # proportion
#> [1] 0.75
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Miscellaneous operators

#### Membership: `%in%`

Tests whether each element on the left appears in the vector on the right.

``` r
c("a", "z") %in% c("a", "b", "c")
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE
```

#### Sequence operator `:`

``` r
1:5
#> [1] 1 2 3 4 5
5:1
#> [1] 5 4 3 2 1
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Indexing and extraction

| Operator | Use | Example |
|------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| `[ ]` | Subset a vector, matrix, or data frame | `x[2]`, `x[-1]`, `x[x > 2]` |
| `[[ ]]` | Extract a single element from a list | `list[["a"]]` |
| `$` | Extract a named element or column | `df$height` |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Note:** x\[i\] and x\[\[i\]\] are equivalent when used on vectors and arrays.

> **Note:** Indexing starts from 1.

> **Note:** x\[\] returns the entire vector.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Examples

``` r
x <- c(a = 10, b = 20, c = 30)

x[2]            # by position
#>  b 
#> 20

x[-1]           # drop the first
#>  b  c 
#> 20 30

x[c(1, 3)]      # list of integers
#>  a  c
#> 10 30
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Examples

``` r
x[c(T, T, F)]   # list of logicals
#>  a  b
#> 10 20

x[x > 15]       # by condition
#>  b  c 

#> 20 30
x["c"]          # by name (if named)
#>  c 
#> 30
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Control flow

#### If-else

``` r
  if (x > 90) {
    "A"
  } else if (x > 80) {
    "B"
  } else if (x > 50) {
    "C"
  } else {
    "F"
  }
```

Since if returns a value, you can also use it as a ternary operator:

```r
x1 <- if (TRUE) 1 else 2
x2 <- if (FALSE) 1 else 2

c(x1, x2)
#> [1] 1 2
```

---

#### ifelse() - a vectorized version of if

```r
x <- 1:10
ifelse(x %% 5 == 0, "XXX", as.character(x))
#>  [1] "1"   "2"   "3"   "4"   "XXX" "6"   "7"   "8"   "9"   "XXX"
```

### Switch-case

```r
  switch(x,
    a = "option 1",
    b = "option 2",
    c = "option 3",
    "option 4" # default value
  )
```

---

> **Note:** Since the focus of the labs is statistic we'll be avoiding
explicint looping in favour of functionals.

### For-loops

```r
for (i in 1:3) {
  print(i)
}
#> [1] 1
#> [1] 2
#> [1] 3
```

The *next* and *break* keywords function like in C++

---

#### Related tools:

while(condition) action: performs action while condition is TRUE.

repeat(action): repeats action forever (or until it encounters break).

---

### Functions

Functions are first-class objects. You create them with `function()` and assign
them to a name, or you can use them as anonymous functions.

``` r
square <- function(x) {
  x^2
}

square(4)
#> [1] 16

(function(x) x + 1)(2)
#> [1] 3
```

The value of the last evaluated expression is returned automatically.
You can return explicitly with `return()`, e.g. if you need the function to
exit early.

---

#### Arguments

Arguments can have **default values** and can 
be passed by **name** or by **position**.

``` r
power <- function(x, exponent = 2) {
  x^exponent
}

power(3)                  # default exponent
#> [1] 9
power(3, 3)               # by position
#> [1] 27
power(exponent = 3, x = 2)  # by name, any order
#> [1] 8
```

Functions are vectorized automatically when they are built from vectorized 
operators:

``` r
power(1:5)
#> [1]  1  4  9 16 25
```

---

### Matrices & Arrays

A **matrix** is an atomic vector with a `dim`
attribute (rows and columns). It can only hold one data type, just like a vector.

``` r
m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, ncol = 3)
m
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    3    5
#> [2,]    2    4    6
```

R fills matrices **column by column**. Use `byrow = TRUE` to fill by row.

``` r
matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    2    3
#> [2,]    4    5    6
```

---

Combine vectors or matrices with `rbind()` (stack rows) 
and `cbind()` (join columns):

``` r
rbind(c(1, 2, 3), c(4, 5, 6))
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    1    2    3
#> [2,]    4    5    6

cbind(a = 1:3, b = c(10, 20, 30))
#>      a  b
#> [1,] 1 10
#> [2,] 2 20
#> [3,] 3 30
```

---

#### Indexing matrices

Use `matrix[row, column]`.

> **Note** Leaving one empty selects everything in that dimension.

``` r
m[2, 3]      # single element
#> [1] 6
m[1, ]       # first row
#> [1] 1 3 5
m[, 2]       # second column
#> [1] 3 4
m[, c(1, 3)] # columns 1 and 3
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    5
#> [2,]    2    6
```

---

#### Arrays

An **array** generalizes matrices to any number of dimensions.

``` r
a <- array(1:24, dim = c(2, 3, 4))
dim(a)
#> [1] 2 3 4
```

> **Note:** A matrix is simply a 2-dimensional array, and a vector has no
`dim` attribute at all.

---

### Sampling

`sample(x, size, replace = FALSE, prob = NULL)` draws a random 
sample of elements from a vector.

| Argument | Meaning |
|:---------|:--------|
| `x` | The vector to sample from |
| `size` | How many elements to draw (defaults to `length(x)`) |
| `replace` | Sample with replacement? (defaults to `FALSE`) |
| `prob` | Optional vector of sampling probabilities |

---

#### Repeating a simulation: `replicate()`

`replicate(n, expr)` evaluates `expr` **n separate times** and collects the
results. It is the standard tool for simulations. We can estimate a probability
by taking the mean of a logical vector:

```r
## Exercise 1
is_same_ball <- function() {
  box <- 1:8
  size <- 2
  replace <- T
  
  result <- sample(box, size, replace)
  result[1] == result[2]
}

number_reps <- 10 ^ 4
mean(replicate(number_reps, is_same_ball()))
```

---

### Some more useful functions

`rep()` repeats the elements of a vector.

``` r
rep(c("a", "b"), times = 3)
#> [1] "a" "b" "a" "b" "a" "b"
```

`seq()` builds vectors

``` r
seq(from = 0, to = 1, by = 0.25)
#> [1] 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00
```

`distinct()` shows which values are distinct

``` r
distinct(c(1, 2, 1))
#> [1] FALSE TRUE FALSE
```

`unique()` creates a vector of unique values from the given vector

``` r
unique(c(1, 2, 1))
#> [1] 1 2
```
